Doctor Anywhere · Identity & Onboarding
Design case study · Shipped, phased over 8 months

Identity-first onboarding

Identity verification at Doctor Anywhere — a project that sits at the intersection of patient safety, regulatory need, and conversion. I led the end-to-end patient experience across onboarding and verification, moving identity from something checked too late to the first thing the system establishes.

8mo1 designer, 2 PMs, 6 engineers
1M+users verified through the new flow
26%of quarterly CS tickets were onboarding-related
Liveshipped · dependents phase in progress
01 — Problem

Not just a real person — the right person

The core problem was not simply verifying that someone is a real person. In telehealth, we need confidence that the person joining the consultation is the enrolled patient, so the right diagnosis, prescription, and medical record go to the right person.

Before this work, onboarding contributed to 26% of customer-support tickets each quarter. New-user onboarding alone accounted for 10 percentage points of that. That told us this wasn't just a compliance or profile-data issue — the journey itself was creating enough uncertainty and friction that patients needed help to get through it.

Identity was being captured too late, or inconsistently, across journeys. That created inaccurate patient information, real support effort, and — at the sharpest edge — the risk of a consultation being linked to the wrong identity.

The challenge wasn't only technical. It was introducing stronger verification without making a patient feel delayed or distrusted right before speaking to a doctor.

Patients are often unwell or anxious. This is not a normal sign-up flow where we can casually add more steps.The constraint that shaped every decision below

This first surfaced as a How Might We on onboarding — the tickets were high, and a large share were coverage complaints: users who couldn't see their benefits, or saw the wrong ones. The proximate cause was routing: Doctor Anywhere ran on two backends, Vantage (Keycloak, corporate/coverage) and AP1 (Firebase, direct/telehealth), and onboarding routed people between them by asking users to self-declare — sign up as "public" or "covered by company benefits." People got it wrong constantly, and identity verification itself only happened after sign-up, not before.

That risk wasn't only a patient-trust problem — it had a regulatory edge too:

Why this became non-negotiable, not just annoying NEHR (National Electronic Health Record) keys every patient record to NRIC/FIN. The Health Information Bill made NEHR contribution mandatory for telemedicine providers starting early 2027, and MOH Circular 87/2024 requires tracking repeat MC issuance per patient. Both assume one clean, deduplicated identity per person — which a self-declared, post-hoc-verified sign-up flow could not reliably produce.
02 — Understanding it

Mapping the full journey, not just the happy path

I mapped new users, existing users, manual ID verification, Singpass verification, failed selfie attempts, and dependent verification — not only the clean path through.

Working with Operations and Engineering, I traced where people were actually dropping off, which failures were recoverable, and which information we could reliably extract rather than asking a patient to type again. That's systems thinking, not just screen design — the shape of the eventual solution came directly out of this mapping, not before it.

One thing that mapping made obvious: this wasn't a B2B problem. Once a patient reaches the video consultation itself — booking, the call, medication, what the doctor sees on their side — a corporate patient and a public patient are doing exactly the same thing. The only place they diverge is payment: one bills to an employer's coverage, the other pays directly. Onboarding and verification genuinely differ by user group, for a real reason — coverage has to be checked, a corporate identity has to be confirmed against an employer. But the consultation experience was never supposed to be two products. It became two by accident, because the account-type split happened at sign-up and nothing downstream ever undid it.

That's the honest answer to "how did you know this wasn't a B2B issue anymore" — not one workshop or one ticket, but tracing a single patient all the way through the journey and noticing the split only mattered at one narrow point.

03 — My role

Owning it end to end, on a small team

I led the end-to-end patient experience across onboarding and identity verification — from the first sign-up screen through to the doctor confirming who they're speaking to. That meant working closely with Product, Engineering, Operations, and compliance stakeholders, not designing screens in isolation.

Sole designer on this project, working alongside 2 PMs and 6 engineers over 8 months. Concretely, that meant:

  • Flow logic and edge cases. Owned the sign-up routing logic end to end, plus every edge-case screen — mid-verification exit, NRIC already registered, MyInfo technical failure.
  • The trade-off calls. The Effort 1 vs. Effort 2 debate on the flow diagram, and the later email/coverage trade-offs with the business side, were mine to resolve, not hand off.
  • Operations-facing decisions. Ran the Security Decision Request process for identity-sensitive edge cases with compliance at the table, and the structured post-launch retro with Operations after launch.
  • The current work. Drafting the dependent-account PRD now — the one population left with no identity check of their own.
04 — Principles

The decision framework behind every choice below

Five principles did the actual work of deciding what to build, in what order, and where to draw the line.

  1. Verify early enough to prevent downstream errors.
  2. Ask only for information we cannot obtain reliably.
  3. Keep the patient moving toward care, not toward an admin task.
  4. Make failure and recovery paths as considered as the ideal path.
  5. Design differently for adult patients and parent-managed dependents.
05 — Evolution

This took three tries — deliberately, not all at once

Given the safety and operational risk, we didn't launch everything together. We rolled out in phases — starting with the core verification journey, then refining specific areas such as manual ID flows, selfie verification, and dependent journeys.

That let us validate each change against real behaviour, monitor support and failure patterns, and improve the experience without exposing every patient to an untested end-to-end change at once. Read the phases left to right — each one solved something and deliberately left something unsolved for the next.

Phase 1 — Past

Two entry points, split by self-declaration. Solved a simple mental model; left wrong-path routing and no identity check at all.

Phase 1.1 — Present, at the time

Started merging the two sign-ups into one. Partial fix — still no verification step before account creation.

Phase 2 — Shipped

Singpass verification moved to the front of the flow. Solved confident identification and MOH alignment; dependent linking and delete-account still open.

If the question is "why not launch it all together?" Because this touched regulated identity data, consultation access, multiple technical dependencies, and operational recovery. A phased release was the responsible choice — it reduced risk, gave clear learning signals, and let the team focus on the highest-friction areas first, instead of guessing which ones those would be.
06 — Decision: identity-first

Identity-first onboarding

We moved identity verification earlier in onboarding. That let the system recognize user context sooner — for example, whether someone might be eligible for company benefits — and avoid creating inaccurate or duplicate profiles downstream.

Why not just verify identity at the point of consultation?

We considered collecting identity only when a user needed a video consultation. That would reduce the first-time barrier — but it solves only one use case. In Doctor Anywhere's ecosystem, a user may come to submit a claim, access company benefits, find a panel clinic, or manage coverage — sometimes before they ever need a consultation.

We also considered a traditional "sign up first, link benefits later" approach. But that assumes a public user later becomes a corporate one. In our ecosystem, many corporate members are new to Doctor Anywhere entirely — asking them to enter through a generic public journey and discover benefits later creates an unnecessary detour, not a simpler one.

We chose identity-first onboarding because it lets us recognize a user's context early and tailor the next step accordingly. A user with eligible benefits should feel they've entered a benefits experience from the start; a public user should continue through a simple consumer journey. The system adapts without asking users to understand our internal product structure.

Alternatives considered

ApproachBenefitWhy it was not enough
Create account first; verify only before a video consultationLowest onboarding friction for users who are browsingDoctor Anywhere is not only a video-consult app. Users may submit claims, view benefits, find panel clinics, or manage coverage before ever booking a consultation.
Let users log in, then link coverage when neededFamiliar model; keeps initial sign-up simpleIt assumes a public B2C user later becomes a B2B member. In reality, many B2B members are completely new to the app and should enter a benefits-led journey from day one.
Ask everyone to select B2C or B2BClear branching on paperIt places an internal business distinction on the user. Many users don't know their eligibility, insurer arrangement, or whether benefits are already linked to their identity.
Separate B2B and B2C appsHighly tailored journeysRecreates the fragmentation Doctor Anywhere is trying to solve: separate accounts, duplicated profiles, unclear ownership, and inconsistent care journeys.
Identity-first onboarding — chosen directionEstablishes identity and eligibility early, then adapts the journeyRequires careful handling of privacy, fallback verification, and failure recovery — but gives the most scalable foundation.
One app does not mean one journey. It means one trusted identity and account foundation, with the right experience surfaced for each person.The senior-product principle underneath this decision

We shouldn't squeeze every user need into one "main" onboarding path. In a scalable ecosystem, there can be one shared identity foundation — but the journey after that should adapt based on the user's verified context, intent, and eligibility.

This is the actual flow diagram from the handoff file, with two design notes attached directly to it — the real trade-off conversation, not a reconstruction.

Effort 1 (rejected): "We are not swapping screens — we should apply Singpass to collect email, it's a new application."Rejected
Effort 2 (adopted): "Instead of swapping screens we can build the system which is not creating account before we store any information."Adopted — the harder, more correct option

We chose the harder, more correct option — don't create an account at all until identity is confirmed — over the cheaper UI-only patch.

07 — Decision: less typing

Minimise manual data entry

Where ID data could be extracted or verified directly — through Singpass, or from the ID document itself — we cut form fields rather than asking a patient to retype what the system could already read.

The intent wasn't only speed. Fewer manual fields also meant fewer transcription errors, and the experience felt more trustworthy — the system already seemed to know who you were, rather than interrogating you. The clearest example is the pre-filled review screen a few sections down, in the recovery-states walkthrough.

08 — Decision: parallel, not gated

Verification in parallel with consultation joining

One important decision was to avoid presenting verification as a hard pause before care. We designed the joining experience so verification could run while the consultation was being prepared in parallel, instead of gating the call behind it.

That mattered on two levels. Operationally, it absorbed the real latency of ID and liveness checks without adding it to the patient's wait. Experientially, it meant the patient felt like they were already moving toward the doctor, not stuck in an admin queue immediately before something they were often anxious about to begin with.

09 — Decision: recovery, considered

Clear recovery for failure states

A failed selfie or ID scan is high-friction and emotionally sensitive. We designed the feedback to be specific and actionable — what happened, what the patient can try next, and when support is needed — rather than a generic "verification failed."

This is also where verification runs a second time: right before the GP, not just at sign-up — because "verified once" only means something if it's still true when a doctor is relying on it. Singpass gives trustworthy text data but no photo of the ID itself, so even a fully Singpass-verified user still needs an ID upload as the reference photo a live selfie gets checked against.

Step 1

Personal details

Retrieved via Singpass or entered manually — establishes what the system is told.

Step 2

ID upload

Document authenticity, checked by an AI service in every region — establishes a real, matching reference photo.

Step 3

Selfie / liveness

Confirms it's really them (a live person) and it's them (matches step 2's reference face).

Same pattern, different moment A returning NRIC still triggers the "this ID is already registered" handoff here, just like it does at sign-up — the same duplicate-identity logic reused rather than rebuilt for this second checkpoint.
What's honestly unconfirmed A distinct, lighter-touch re-verification path specifically for already-verified returning patients wasn't clearly present as its own flow in this file — worth confirming directly rather than assuming it exists.
10 — Decision: a different model

Dependent experience

Dependents needed a different mental model entirely. A parent completes the action, but the identity belongs to the child — so the flow can't just be the adult flow with a smaller font.

We reduced unnecessary input for a child's profile, used parent-aware language throughout ("you're verifying for [child's name]," not "verify your identity"), and adjusted tone so it read as reassuring without becoming childish.

This work is still in progress. I'm currently drafting the PRD that extends full identity verification to dependents directly, with an age-gated selfie rule (0–6 exempt, 7–16 required) — the one population today without an identity check of their own, and the direct throughline from the post-launch retro in Outcomes below.

11 — User journey & service mapping

What actually happens when identity fails — and what replaces it

Not an abstract journey map — the real B2B scenario: a corporate patient goes to see a GP, and identity either resolves before that visit or doesn't. Both paths, mapped in full.

Coverage vanishes from identity drift
  • AP1 (telehealth) and Vantage (coverage) can each hold a slightly different NRIC/email for the same member. When they drift, the Coverage tab disappears with no warning.
Out of pocket, then a TPA claim
  • When benefit-matching fails, the patient isn't told at sign-up — they find out at the point of care, pay out of pocket, and file a claim that lands on the payers team as manual reconciliation.

Recurring across ESD-9317, ESD-9431, ESD-9527, ESD-9693, ESD-9895. Scale: 112,844 active B2B policies unregistered across 9 tenants — 17,051 of those belong to members who already have a DA account under a different identity.

Why early identification matters most for corporate users The moment identity resolves to "corporate, employer X" moved from after account creation to before it — steps 1–3 in the after-flow now happen before the patient ever books a GP. Coverage, GP panel, and pricing are already contextual by the time the patient reaches the doctor. From step 4 onward, the flow is identical for every patient — this is the video consultation experience staying one product instead of two.

13 — Outcomes

Where it landed, from first evidence to company impact

We shipped and monitored the core verification flow closely after release. In the early monitoring window, 930 users completed verification successfully, 56 were blocked at the selfie step, and Operations directly supported 6 cases.

More importantly, this gave a clear view of where the real friction actually was, so the recovery flow could be improved from evidence rather than assumption — which fed directly into the retro below.

Post-launch retro10 blockers
Most blockers traced back to one issue
What happened
"After launch, we identified 10 quality blockers. Through root cause analysis, we found most traced back to some core issue." Logged in #temp-exp-quality-review with each blocker owned by a team (BD, GHS) and threaded to resolution.
Root cause
Dependent accounts couldn't be promoted to independent login accounts (PAO-3061, flagged Highest priority).
Fix
Fixed the backend flow and designed clearer error states in parallel — shipped incrementally rather than waiting for a single perfect release.

Zooming out

This project addressed a meaningful support burden: onboarding had represented 26% of quarterly customer-support tickets, including 10 points from new users alone. By treating identity verification as a phased product capability rather than a one-time compliance screen, we could reduce that uncertainty progressively while protecting patient safety and maintaining a smooth path to care.

At a company level, this strengthens the foundation for safe telehealth, accurate patient records, smoother benefits eligibility, and scalable onboarding across B2C, B2B, and dependent journeys. It's a foundational capability, not a one-off compliance feature.

1M+users verified through the new identity flow
26%of quarterly CS tickets were onboarding-related, 10 points from new users alone
0manual re-linking steps for correctly matched B2B coverage
2027-ready: stronger MOH/NEHR alignment ahead of the mandatory-contribution deadline

What this actually fixed

  • Coverage no longer disappears from identity drift. Resolving identity once, correctly, before an account exists removes the AP1↔Vantage mismatch that used to make the Coverage tab silently vanish.
  • Corporate users stop paying out of pocket at the point of care. Coverage is confirmed before the GP visit, not discovered to be broken during it.
  • Providers aren't forced to mark consults incomplete. The three-layer confidence model means a provider is looking at a verified identity, not an unconfirmed one.
  • Faster, smoother consultations where Singpass verification was already completed before the visit.
14 — What I'd do differently

Two calls I'd make differently next time

Looking back, I would have brought structured usability validation of the failure states earlier into the process — particularly lower-quality ID capture, repeated selfie failures, and parent-managed dependent flows.

We designed these carefully, but production behaviour surfaced nuances that a broader set of realistic scenarios could have revealed sooner. I now treat operational failure data as an input to the design process from the start, not only as post-launch monitoring.

I also initially explored a more detailed, sequential loading reveal, to make the verification system feel transparent while it worked. But it risked making a short wait feel longer, and drew attention to the verification mechanics rather than away from them. We chose a simpler skeleton-loading approach instead.

Transparency should reassure a patient, not make them watch the system work.The lesson from that trade-off
15 — Where my judgment shifted

What I got wrong, and what changed

My early instinct was to make every verification step highly visible, so patients understood exactly what was happening. In a care context, that instinct was wrong — too much process visibility increased anxiety instead of reducing it.

The better outcome wasn't more explanation everywhere. It was the right explanation at moments of real uncertainty, with the rest of the experience feeling calm and fast. That's a judgment I only trust now because I watched the more-visible version land worse.
